Carmen. Georges Bizet's Carmen, composed in 1875, is a four-act French opera that stands as one of the most popular and frequently performed works in the classical canon. Based on Prosper Mérimée's novella, the opera is set in Seville, Spain, and follows the downfall of Don José, a naive soldier who is seduced by the fiery, free-spirited gypsy Carmen. Don José deserts his military post and abandons his childhood sweetheart, Micaëla, to join Carmen's band of smugglers, only to be rejected when she falls for the glamorous bullfighter Escamillo. Infuriated by jealousy, Don José murders Carmen outside the bullring. The opera's premiere at the Opéra-Comique in Paris was initially a critical failure, scandalizing audiences with its gritty realism, but it quickly achieved global acclaim shortly after Bizet's untimely death.

Carmen is a seductive gypsy cigarette-factory worker who fiercely values her freedom. She sings the famous Habanera to assert her philosophy of love. Don José is a corporal in the military who falls under Carmen's spell, eventually mutinying, joining smugglers, and ultimately stabbing her to death in a fit of jealous rage. Escamillo is a dashing bullfighter from Granada who becomes Don José's rival for Carmen's affections. Micaëla is a loyal village girl and Don José's childhood sweetheart who travels to the smugglers' mountain hideout to plead with him to visit his dying mother. Zuniga is Don José's lieutenant who also desires Carmen; Don José attacks him, forcing himself to desert the army and flee with the smugglers.

The Habanera, titled L'amour est un oiseau rebelle, is Carmen's entrance aria in Act One, characterized by its descending chromatic scale and habanera rhythm, adapting a melody by Sebastián Yradier. The Toreador Song, or Votre toast, je peux vous le rendre, is Escamillo's Act Two aria celebrating the drama and glory of the bullring. The Seguidilla, Près des remparts de Séville, is sung by Carmen in Act One to seduce Don José into releasing her from custody. The Flower Song, La fleur que tu m'avais jetée, is Don José's Act Two aria in which he presents Carmen with a dried flower she threw at him, declaring his devotion. The Card Aria, En vain pour éviter, occurs in Act Three when Carmen joins her friends Frasquita and Mercédès in fortune-telling, only to repeatedly draw cards foretelling her own death and Don José's.

Carmen was pioneering in its realistic portrayal of the working class, lawlessness, and tragic sexuality on the operatic stage, defying the conventions of the traditional opéra comique genre. Its music, which Bizet infused with Spanish folk idioms despite never visiting Spain, has become deeply embedded in popular culture, appearing in countless advertisements, films, and parodies. The opera also inspired a famous 1943 Broadway musical adaptation, Carmen Jones, with lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein the Second, and a ballet adaptation by Rodion Shchedrin. Georges Bizet was a prominent French composer of the Romantic era.
